newsitem.title: GERMANY: Iran leaders ordered Berlin killing, court says.
newsitem.headline: Iran leaders ordered Berlin killing, court says.

text.p: A German court on Thursday accused Iran's leaders of ordering the assassination of a group of Iranian Kurdish exiles in a gangland-style slaying in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant in 1992.

It was not immediately clear whether the court, which handed down life sentences to the two main suspects and long jail sentences to two accomplices, would name the Iranian leaders it thought were behind the killings.

But the link looked sure to infuriate the Islamic republic, which denied all responsibility when prosecutors alleged supreme religious leader Ayatollah Ali Khameni ordered the killings and President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani approved them.
Germany has already issued an arrest warrant for Iranian Intelligence Minister Ali Fallahiyan in connection with the killings.
"Iran's political leadership ordered the crime," presiding judge Frithjof Kubsch said.

Kubsch gave life sentences to Kazem Darabi, an Iranian, and Abbas Rhayel, a Lebanese, for the murder of Sadegh Sharafkandi, exiled leader of the Iranian Democratic Party of Kurdistan, and two fellow officials and a translator.
Two other Lebanese got prison sentences of between five and 11 years as accomplices and a fifth suspect was cleared.
Various Iranian politicians and religious leaders have accused Germany of orchestrating a political trial.
Germany, Iran's biggest trading partner and most important friend in the West, has said the outcome of the trial may force it to review its relations with Iran.
Bonn has until now doggedly insisted on maintaining amicable relations while its major allies, above all Britain and the United States, accuse the Iranians of state terrorism.
But last year the German Foreign Ministry urged Germans not to go to Iran unless absolutely necessary, and then to stay in constant touch with the embassy.

Media reports said a government working group expected Iran's reaction to the judgment to be limited if Tehran were mentioned only in general terms as the originator of the attack, but much more severe if Rafsanjani or Khameni were named.

Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati was quoted by the Iranian daily Kayhan on Wednesday as saying that "a negative verdict by the Mykonos trial will have a negative impact on political and economic ties between Tehran and Bonn".
But he denied that pro-Iranian groups might attack German interests or German nationals in Iran, saying: "We support human values and German nationals will have full security."

Western diplomats have said the verdict comes at a bad time -- just a month before a presidential election in Iran which is forcing even moderate politicians such as those in the Foreign Ministry to espouse the tougher line of the conservative clergy.

Iran was particularly incensed that the prosecution based many of its assertions on the testimony of former president Abolhassan Banisadr and of Abolhassem Mesbahi, until recently an international trouble-shooter for Tehran, and now, like Banisadr, a fugitive from its wrath.

Mesbahi told the court that written orders for assassinations such as the one in Berlin were issued by a secret Council for Special Operations, chaired by Khamenei. The orders would be approved by Rafsanjani, he said.
